claims.text: The catalytic performance of transition-metal catalysts is governed by the position of the d-band center relative to the Fermi level.
Shifting the d-band center toward an optimum position enhances adsorption of key reaction intermediates.
Optimizing intermediate adsorption by shifting the d-band center boosts catalytic activity.
Optimizing intermediate adsorption by shifting the d-band center improves selectivity.
An optimum d-band-center shift can improve performance while maintaining durability.
An excessive d-band-center shift causes overly strong adsorption.
Overly strong adsorption impedes catalytic turnover and reduces catalyst life.
Introducing a controlled amount of a second metal through alloying or doping systematically shifts the d-band center.
Alloying or doping can alter electronic structure without substantially changing particle morphology or support interaction.
The d-band-center position determines the binding strengths of reaction intermediates on the catalyst surface.
Doping or alloying can shift the d-band center closer to or farther from the Fermi level.
Changes in the d-band center adjust adsorption energies of key intermediates.
Changes in intermediate adsorption energies modulate reaction activation barriers.
An optimally positioned d-band center stabilizes intermediates without causing poisoning.
Avoiding poisoning while adequately stabilizing intermediates improves catalytic turnover and selectivity.
Catalysts with an optimally shifted d-band center will exhibit greater activity than the baseline pure-metal catalyst.
Catalysts with an optimally shifted d-band center will exhibit better selectivity than the baseline pure-metal catalyst.
An extreme d-band-center shift will reduce turnover rates and accelerate deactivation.
The hypothesis applies to transition-metal catalysts whose behavior is largely controlled by adsorption energetics described by d-band theory.
The hypothesis is expected to hold under moderate-temperature conditions that do not cause significant sintering or phase transformation.
